lessons.title: Science in Our Daily Lives
learn: Science is all around us — it helps us understand why things happen and how to make life easier and safer.
We use science every day: cooking involves chemistry, riding a bike involves physics, and taking medicine involves biology.

Famous scientists and their inventions: Thomas Edison (light bulb), Alexander Graham Bell (telephone), Marie Curie (research on radioactivity), Isaac Newton (laws of motion), and Louis Pasteur (pasteurization, which keeps milk safe to drink).
Scientists are curious people who ask questions, observe carefully, and test their ideas through experiments.

lessons.title: Science Process Skills
learn: Science process skills are the basic skills scientists use: observing, measuring, classifying, predicting, and communicating.
Observing means using your five senses to gather information about the world.
Measuring means using tools to find exact amounts — like length, mass, temperature, or time — instead of just guessing.

Common science tools: thermometer (temperature), ruler or tape measure (length), weighing scale (mass), magnifying glass (small details), beaker and graduated cylinder (liquid volume), and stopwatch (time).
Using the right tool makes observations far more accurate than estimating by eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Changes in Properties of Matter

lessons.title: How Physical Change in Matter Occurs
learn: A physical change alters the size, shape, or state of matter, but the substance stays the same kind of matter.
Heating and cooling can cause phase changes: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation (liquid to gas), and condensation (gas to liquid).
Examples: ice melting into water, water boiling into steam, folding paper, cutting cloth, or dissolving sugar in water (it's still sugar and water, just mixed together).
Physical changes are usually easy to reverse — melted ice can be frozen back into ice.

lessons.title: How Chemical Change in Matter Occurs
learn: A chemical change happens when matter transforms into a new substance with different properties — this cannot easily be undone.
Signs of a chemical change: a color change, gas bubbles forming, heat or light being released, a new smell, or a solid forming from liquids.
Examples: burning paper (turns to ash and smoke), rusting of iron, cooking an egg, milk turning sour, or mixing baking soda and vinegar (produces bubbling gas).
Some chemical changes are useful (cooking food) while others can be undesirable, like rusting metal or spoiling food.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Human and Plant Body Systems

lessons.title: Human Body Systems
learn: The circulatory system pumps blood through the body using the heart and blood vessels, delivering oxygen and nutrients.
The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients the body can use, starting at the mouth and ending at the intestines.
The muscular system allows the body to move — muscles work by contracting and relaxing.
The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide, mainly through the lungs.
The skeletal system is made of bones that support the body, protect organs, and work together with muscles to create movement.

lessons.title: Plant Body System
learn: A typical plant has two main systems: the root system (underground) and the shoot system (above ground — stem, leaves, and flowers).
Roots anchor the plant in soil and absorb water and minerals.
The stem supports the plant and transports water and nutrients between the roots and leaves.
Leaves make food for the plant through photosynthesis, using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.
Flowers help plants reproduce by producing seeds.

lessons.title: Animals that Live on Land or in Water
learn: A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, providing food, water, shelter, and space.
Land habitats house animals like lions, rabbits, and ants, which usually have legs for walking or running.
Water habitats — like oceans, rivers, and lakes — house animals like fish, which use gills to breathe underwater.
Animals that fly, like birds and bats, have wings adapted for moving through the air.
Some animals, like frogs and ducks, can live both on land and in water.

lessons.title: Plants that Live on Land or in Water
learn: Land plants, like trees and grasses, have strong roots that anchor them in soil and absorb water from the ground.
Water plants, like water lilies and lotus, often have air pockets or wide, flat leaves that help them float.
Some water plants have roots that hang freely in the water instead of anchoring in soil.
All plants are adapted to their habitat to get enough sunlight, water, and nutrients to survive.

lessons.title: Life Cycles of Some Animals
lessons.sub: Butterfly, Mosquito, Fly, Bee, Frog, Chicken
learn: A life cycle shows the stages an animal goes through from birth to adulthood.
Butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult butterfly.
Mosquito and fly: egg → larva → pupa → adult — often developing in water for mosquitoes.
Frog: egg → tadpole → tadpole with legs → adult frog — a big change from living in water to living on land.
Bee: egg → larva → pupa → adult bee, living together in colonies.
Chicken: egg → chick → adult chicken — mainly just growth, without a dramatic body change.
Environmental changes like pollution, temperature shifts, or habitat loss can disrupt these life cycles.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of Humans
learn: The human life cycle includes these stages: fetus, infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and elderly.
Fetus: the stage of development before birth, inside the mother's womb.
Infancy: from birth to about 2 years old, when a baby learns basic skills like crawling and walking.
Childhood: from about 2 to 12 years old, marked by rapid learning and physical growth.
Adolescence: the teenage years, when the body undergoes puberty and rapid change.
Adulthood: the body is fully grown; people often work, start families, and become more independent.
Elderly: the later stage of life, when the body slows down and may need more care.
Environmental factors like nutrition, healthcare, and safety affect how humans grow through each stage.

lessons.title: Classifying Animals According to the Food They Eat
learn: Living things depend on each other for food, forming connections throughout nature.
Producers (like plants) make their own food using sunlight through photosynthesis.
Consumers cannot make their own food, so they eat other organisms — they include herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores.
Herbivores eat only plants (like cows and rabbits). Carnivores eat only other animals (like lions and eagles). Omnivores eat both plants and animals (like humans and bears).
Decomposers (like fungi and bacteria) break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil.

lessons.title: A Simple Food Chain
learn: A food chain shows how energy passes from one living thing to another, usually starting with a producer.
The primary consumer eats the producer (example: a grasshopper eats grass).
The secondary consumer eats the primary consumer (example: a frog eats the grasshopper).
The tertiary consumer eats the secondary consumer (example: a snake eats the frog).
If one part of the food chain is removed or harmed, it can affect all the other living things connected to it.

lessons.title: Measuring Time and Distance Using Standard Units
learn: Standard units allow everyone to measure things the same way, so measurements can be compared accurately.
Distance is commonly measured in standard units like meters (m) and kilometers (km), using tools like a ruler, meter stick, or tape measure.
Time is measured in standard units like seconds, minutes, and hours, using tools like a clock or stopwatch.
Using standard units instead of things like footsteps or handspans makes measurements consistent no matter who measures them.

lessons.title: Measuring and Graphing Different Speed
learn: Speed tells us how fast something is moving — it is calculated using the distance traveled and the time it takes.
A simple formula: Speed = Distance ÷ Time.
Faster objects cover more distance in the same amount of time compared to slower objects.
Graphs help us compare speeds visually — a steeper line on a distance-time graph means a faster speed.

lessons.title: Effects of Force Applied on Objects
learn: A force is a push or pull that can affect an object's shape, size, speed, or direction.
Force can change an object's speed — making it speed up or slow down.
Force can change an object's direction — like when you kick a ball and it changes course.
Force can change an object's shape — like squeezing clay or stretching a rubber band.
Generally, the stronger the force applied, the greater the effect on the object.

lessons.title: Force Exerted by a Magnet
learn: A magnet is an object that can pull certain materials toward it using an invisible force called magnetism.
Magnets attract materials that contain iron, nickel, or cobalt — like iron nails, paperclips, and some coins.
Magnets do not attract materials like plastic, wood, glass, or paper, since these are not magnetic materials.
Every magnet has two poles: north and south. Like poles repel (push away), and opposite poles attract (pull together).

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Energy: Light, Sound and Heat

lessons.title: Energy from Light
learn: Light is a form of energy that allows us to see objects around us.
Sources of light can be natural (the sun, fire) or artificial (light bulbs, flashlights).
Light travels in straight lines and can be blocked by objects, creating shadows.
Light is important because it lets us see, helps plants make food through photosynthesis, and provides warmth.

lessons.title: Energy from Sound
learn: Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrations that travel through air, water, or solid materials.
Sources of sound include musical instruments, human voices, animals, and machines.
Sound needs a medium (like air) to travel — it cannot travel through empty space (a vacuum).
Sound is important for communication, warning of danger, and enjoying music.

lessons.title: Energy from Heat
learn: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.
Heat can transfer in three ways: conduction (through direct contact), convection (through moving liquids or gases), and radiation (through waves, like heat from the sun).
Sources of heat include the sun, fire, and electrical appliances.
Heat is important for cooking food, keeping our bodies warm, and drying wet things.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Soil and Water in the Environment

lessons.title: Soil in the Environment
lessons.sub: Types of Soil and Water Retention
learn: Soil is the top layer of the earth, made of minerals, organic matter, water, and air.
Different types of soil include sandy soil, clay soil, and loamy soil, each with different textures and abilities to hold water.
Sandy soil has large particles and drains water quickly, holding very little water.
Clay soil has fine particles that hold water well but drain slowly.
Loamy soil is a balanced mix of sand, silt, and clay, making it great for holding water and growing plants.

lessons.title: Importance of Water to Living Things
learn: Water comes from many sources: rain, rivers, lakes, groundwater, and the ocean.
All living things need water to survive — for drinking, growing, and carrying out body processes.
Plants use water (with sunlight) to make their own food through photosynthesis.
Water from different sources is used for drinking, cooking, bathing, irrigation (watering crops), and generating electricity.

lessons.title: Weather
learn: Weather describes the condition of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, including temperature, humidity, wind, and precipitation.
Weather elements include temperature, humidity (moisture in the air), wind, air pressure, and precipitation (rain, snow).
Weather conditions can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, or stormy.
Weather instruments help measure weather elements: a thermometer (temperature), a rain gauge (rainfall amount), an anemometer (wind speed), and a barometer (air pressure).

lessons.title: Weather Forecasting
learn: Weather forecasting is the process of predicting future weather conditions based on collected data.
Weather forecasting is important because it helps people prepare for storms, plan activities, and stay safe.
During different weather conditions, people should follow safety precautions: staying indoors during storms, wearing appropriate clothing, and avoiding flooded areas.
Weather forecasters use tools and data from satellites and weather stations to make their predictions.

lessons.title: The Sun
learn: The sun is a star at the center of our solar system that provides light and heat to Earth.
The sun is extremely hot and made mostly of hydrogen and helium gases.
The sun's energy supports life on Earth by providing warmth and enabling plants to make food.
Too much exposure to the sun can be harmful, causing sunburn or eye damage, so precautions include wearing sunscreen, sunglasses, and hats, and avoiding direct exposure during peak hours.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship
learn: An entrepreneur is a person who starts, organizes, and manages a business, taking on the risks in the hope of earning a profit.
Entrepreneurship is the whole process of planning, setting up, and running a business — from spotting an opportunity to actually offering a product or service.
Entrepreneurship is important because it creates jobs for other people, provides goods and services that communities need, and helps the local economy grow.
Entrepreneurs take risks, but they also plan carefully — they research what people need before starting a business.

chapters.title: B. Qualities of a Successful Entrepreneur

lessons.title: Qualities of a Successful Entrepreneur
learn: Successful entrepreneurs usually share certain qualities: hard work, creativity, resourcefulness, honesty, patience, and the willingness to take calculated risks.
They are also decisive — able to make choices quickly — and persistent, continuing to try even after facing failure.
Filipino entrepreneurs like Henry Sy (SM) and Tony Tan Caktiong (Jollibee) built large businesses by working hard, listening to customers, and improving their products over time.
International entrepreneurs, such as those who built well-known companies, are often known for their creativity and willingness to try new ideas that others thought were impossible.

lessons.title: Types of Businesses and Kinds of Services
learn: Businesses can be classified by ownership: a sole proprietorship is owned by one person, a partnership is owned by two or more people, and a corporation is owned by many shareholders.
Businesses can also be classified by what they offer: some sell goods (like a store selling clothes), while others offer services (like a salon or a repair shop).
Common kinds of services include education, healthcare, transportation, and food service — these do not produce a physical product but provide help or work for a fee.
Choosing the right type of business depends on the entrepreneur's resources, skills, and the needs of the community.

chapters.title: A. Keeping the Home Clean and Beautiful

lessons.title: The Rooms in the House and Cleaning Tools
learn: A home usually has different rooms, each with its own purpose: the living room (for relaxing and receiving guests), bedroom (for sleeping), kitchen (for cooking), dining room (for eating), and bathroom (for hygiene).
Keeping each room clean and organized makes the home healthier, safer, and more pleasant to live in.
Common cleaning tools include a broom and dustpan (sweeping), mop (cleaning floors), rag or cloth (wiping surfaces), and feather duster (removing dust).
Using the right tool for the right task makes cleaning faster and more effective.

chapters.title: B. Taking Care of the Kitchen

lessons.title: Cooking Rice and Cleaning the Kitchen
learn: Preparing and cooking rice properly involves washing the rice, measuring the correct amount of water, and cooking it until it is soft but not mushy.
Cleaning the kitchen and dining area regularly prevents pests, keeps food safe, and makes the space pleasant to cook and eat in.
Dishes and cooking utensils should be washed with soap and water right after use, rinsed well, and dried to prevent bacteria from growing.
A safe kitchen habit is to wipe spills immediately and keep countertops free of clutter.

lessons.title: Introduction to Meal Preparation
learn: Meal preparation is the process of planning, gathering ingredients, and cooking food for a meal.
A good meal plan includes a balance of food groups — like rice or bread (energy), vegetables and fruits (vitamins), and meat, fish, or eggs (protein).
Before cooking, it is important to wash your hands, gather all ingredients, and check that tools and the cooking area are clean.
Following simple steps in order — like a recipe — helps make sure a meal turns out well and safely.

chapters.title: D. Taking Care of One's Clothes

lessons.title: Caring for Clothes and Laundering
lessons.sub: Steps in Laundering, Removing Spots and Stains
learn: Taking care of clothes means storing them properly, mending small tears, and washing them regularly to keep them clean and lasting longer.
The basic steps in laundering are: sorting clothes (by color and fabric), pre-treating stains, washing, rinsing, and drying.
Sorting clothes before washing prevents colors from bleeding onto lighter fabrics.
Removing spots and stains works best when done quickly — using mild soap or a stain remover before the stain sets in.

lessons.title: Recycling
learn: The 3Rs of waste management are Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again), and Recycle (turn waste into something new).
Recyclable products include paper, plastic bottles, cans, and cardboard — materials that can be processed and made into new items.
Having the skill of recycling helps reduce trash, save resources, and protect the environment from pollution.
General steps in making a recycled project: collect clean materials, plan a design, cut and shape the materials, then assemble and decorate the final product.

lessons.title: Basic Mensuration
lessons.sub: Tools for Measuring and Systems of Measurement
learn: Mensuration is the process of measuring things like length, width, and area using tools and standard units.
Common measuring tools include a ruler, tape measure, and meter stick, each useful for different sizes of objects.
Two common systems of measurement are the metric system (meters, centimeters) and the English system (inches, feet).
Choosing the right tool and unit makes measurements more accurate — for example, a tape measure works better than a small ruler for measuring a room.

lessons.title: Lettering
learn: Lettering is the art of drawing letters neatly and consistently, often used for posters, signs, and labels.
Common styles of lettering include block letters (simple, bold), script (flowing, cursive-like), and italic (slanted) letters.
Guidelines — light pencil lines drawn before lettering — help keep letters the same height and evenly spaced.
Proportion in lettering means keeping the width and height of letters balanced so the whole word looks neat and readable.

lessons.title: Alphabet of Lines
lessons.sub: Use of Lines in Orthographic and Isometric Drawing
learn: The 'alphabet of lines' refers to the different types of lines used in technical drawing, each with its own meaning and use.
Common lines include: visible lines (solid, show edges you can see), hidden lines (dashed, show edges you can't see), and center lines (thin, mark the center of a shape).
Orthographic drawing shows an object from flat views — like the front, top, and side — using these standard lines.
Isometric drawing shows an object in 3D, giving it depth so it looks more realistic, while still following standard line rules.

lessons.title: Agriculture and Its Branches
learn: Agriculture is the science and practice of farming, including growing crops and raising animals for food and other products.
Plant raising is an important branch of agriculture because it provides food, materials, and income for many families.
Branches of agriculture include crop production, livestock raising, fishery, and forestry.
The Philippines has laws, local ordinances, and agencies — like the Department of Agriculture — that support and regulate farming to protect farmers and consumers.

chapters.title: B. Garden Tools and Their Uses

lessons.title: Garden Tools and Their Uses
learn: A trowel is a small hand tool used for digging small holes when planting seedlings.
A rake is used to gather leaves, level soil, or remove small stones and debris from the garden.
A watering can or hose is used to water plants evenly without damaging them.
A spade or shovel is used for bigger digging tasks, like turning soil or digging larger holes.
Using the correct garden tool for each task makes gardening safer and more efficient.

lessons.title: Composting
lessons.sub: Making Compost and Its Use and Care
learn: Composting is the process of turning organic waste — like fruit peels, dried leaves, and vegetable scraps — into nutrient-rich soil material.
Steps in composting: collect organic waste, layer it with soil or dry leaves, keep it moist, and turn the pile regularly to help it break down.
Compost takes weeks to months to fully break down into dark, crumbly material that is ready to use.
Finished compost is used to enrich garden soil, helping plants grow healthier, and it should be stored in a cool, slightly moist area.

lessons.title: Ornamental Garden
lessons.sub: Importance, Kinds, and Household Ornamental Plants
learn: Ornamental gardening is growing plants mainly for their beauty rather than for food.
Ornamental gardening is important because it beautifies surroundings, improves air quality, and can even boost people's mood.
Kinds of ornamental gardening include container gardening (plants in pots), landscape gardening (plants arranged in yards), and indoor gardening.
Common household ornamental plants include roses, orchids, ferns, and succulents, chosen for their color, shape, or ease of care.

lessons.title: Vegetable Garden
lessons.sub: Classifications of Vegetable Crops and the Planting Calendar
learn: Vegetable gardening is important because it provides fresh, healthy food, can save money, and teaches responsibility.
Vegetable crops can be classified by the part eaten: leafy vegetables (like lettuce), root crops (like carrots), and fruit vegetables (like tomatoes).
A planting calendar shows the best time of year to plant certain vegetables, based on the local climate and seasons.
Following a planting calendar helps ensure vegetables grow well and produce a good harvest.

mapeh.title: My Cultural Identity and My Province

chapters.title: Dances and Visual Arts of Luzon

lessons.title: Makonggo Dance and the Art of Paper Cutting
lessons.sub: History, Elements of Art and Principles of Design, Pabalat Artwork
learn: The Makonggo Dance comes from Bulacan and imitates the playful movements of a monkey ("unggoy"), performed with lively, comic gestures.
Paper cutting is an intricate art form practiced in Luzon, most famously as Pabalat artwork — delicate designs cut from paper and used to decorate local sweets called pastillas.
The elements of art are the building blocks artists use: line, shape, form, color, space, value, and texture.
Principles of design — like balance, contrast, and proportion — guide how artists arrange the elements of art to create a pleasing artwork.
In Pabalat, careful cutting, symmetry, and color choices combine line, shape, and space to create beautiful decorative patterns.

lessons.title: Visayan Weaving and Boholano Lullabies
learn: The Visayas region is known for artisanal crafts, including basket weaving, which uses local materials like bamboo, rattan, or pandan leaves.
Weaving baskets takes skill and patience, and the craft has been passed down through generations in many Visayan communities.
Boholano lullabies are traditional songs sung to lull babies to sleep, carrying gentle melodies passed down through families.
"Tingkatulog" is a well-known Boholano lullaby song, reflecting the soft, soothing musical style typical of lullabies from Bohol.

chapters.title: Celebrations and Legacy of Mindanao and Beyond

lessons.title: Hermosa Festival and the Artistic Expression of Mindanao
learn: The Hermosa Festival is a religious and cultural celebration with a history rooted in devotion, often featuring processions, music, and community gatherings.
Mindanao is known for rich, colorful artistic expression, including intricate weaving, brasswork, and vibrant traditional patterns influenced by its diverse cultural groups.
Artistic traditions from Mindanao often carry symbolic meanings tied to nature, community identity, and spirituality.
Celebrations like the Hermosa Festival help communities preserve and pass on their cultural identity to younger generations.

lessons.title: Hudhud: Bulul and the Province of Ifugao
learn: Hudhud refers to a tradition of chants from the Ifugao people, often recited during harvest season, funerals, or other important events.
Bulul is a carved wooden figure considered the Ifugao's rice deity, believed to protect and bless the rice harvest.
Ifugao province, located in the Cordillera region, is famous for its centuries-old rice terraces carved into the mountains.
The traditions of Hudhud and Bulul show how deeply agriculture — especially rice farming — is connected to Ifugao culture and spirituality.

lessons.title: Tanghal: National Theater Festival
lessons.sub: Marinduque, Singkil, Mindanao — Land of Promise
learn: "Tanghal" refers to the National Theater Festival, a celebration that showcases Philippine performing arts, including dance, music, and drama from different regions.
Marinduque, often called "The Heart of the Philippines," is known for its unique cultural traditions and festivals, including the Moriones Festival.
Singkil is a traditional Maranao dance that tells a story using bamboo poles that are clapped together in rhythm, while dancers step gracefully between them.
Mindanao is often called the "Land of Promise" because of its rich natural resources and diverse cultural heritage.

mapeh.title: Legends and Folklore of My Province or Region

chapters.title: Mythology, Legends, and the Ancient Lake

lessons.title: Philippine Mythology, Legends, and Lanao Lake
learn: Philippine mythology and legends are traditional stories that explain the origins of places, natural events, or cultural practices, often passed down orally.
"Spectacle" in performance refers to the visual elements — costumes, sets, movement — while "sound" includes music, chants, and voice used to tell a story.
Lanao Lake, one of the oldest and largest lakes in the Philippines, has legends surrounding its formation, often tied to Maranao oral tradition.
These legends are important because they preserve a community's values, history, and identity across generations.

lessons.title: Character, Movement, Melody, and the Higantes Festival
learn: In storytelling and performance, "character" refers to who or what is being portrayed, "movement" is how they act or move, and "melody" is the musical tune that accompanies the story.
Puppets are often used in celebrations to bring characters to life in a visual, playful way, especially during festivals.
The Higantes Festival in Angono, Rizal, features giant paper-mache puppets called "higantes," paraded through the streets to honor the town's patron saint.
The Higantes originated as a way for farmers to playfully mock Spanish landlords during the colonial period, and today they represent local pride and creativity.

lessons.title: Kadayawan Festival and the Masskara Festival
learn: The Kadayawan Festival, celebrated in Davao, is a thanksgiving celebration for a bountiful harvest, featuring music, dance, and displays of local fruits and flowers.
Music plays a central role in Kadayawan, with drumbeats and traditional instruments accompanying street dances and parades.
The Masskara Festival, celebrated in Bacolod, is known for its colorful smiling masks, symbolizing the resilience and cheerful spirit of its people.
Both festivals show how celebrations use art, music, and costume to express a community's identity and values.

chapters.title: Concept and Practices of Personal Health

lessons.title: Personal Health and Hygiene Practices
lessons.sub: Body Care, Sense Organs, Oral Care
learn: Personal health refers to taking care of your body so you can stay active, strong, and free from illness.
Personal health is important for active living — a healthy body allows you to play, learn, and enjoy daily activities.
Body care and hygiene include regular bathing, washing hands, and wearing clean clothes to prevent germs from spreading.
Caring for the sense organs (eyes, ears, nose) means protecting them from injury and getting regular check-ups.
Oral care involves brushing your teeth at least twice a day and visiting the dentist regularly to prevent cavities and gum problems.

lessons.title: Health Appraisal, Vision, Hearing, and Dental Check-ups
learn: Health appraisal procedures are regular check-ups that assess a person's current health status, including height, weight, vision, hearing, and dental health.
Vision check-ups help detect problems like blurry sight early, so they can be corrected with glasses or treatment.
Hearing check-ups help identify hearing problems early, which is important for learning and communication.
Dental check-ups help catch cavities or gum problems early, before they become more serious.
Being aware of your body's health status helps you and your family take action early if something needs attention.

chapters.title: Traditional Games and A Healthy Family

lessons.title: Habulan Estatwa and Araw Lilim
lessons.sub: Chasing Statue, A-An-Ang and Holen, Palm Wrestling
learn: "Habulan Estatwa" (Chasing Statue) is a traditional Filipino game where players freeze like a statue when the "it" player looks at them, and move again once unseen.
"Araw Lilim" involves players trying to stay in the shade ("lilim") to avoid being tagged by the player who is "it" while in the sun ("araw").
"A-An-Ang" and "Holen" are traditional marble games where players try to hit opponents' marbles or reach a target using flicking or shooting techniques.
Palm wrestling is a simple traditional game of strength where two players try to push down each other's palm or arm.
These traditional games build physical skills like agility, balance, and strength, while also teaching fair play and teamwork.

lessons.title: A Healthy Family
learn: A healthy family is one where members support, communicate, and care for each other physically, emotionally, and socially.
Characteristics of a healthy family include open communication, mutual respect, shared responsibilities, and spending quality time together.
Promoting a healthy family is important because it creates a safe, supportive environment where children can grow and thrive.
Each family member has roles and responsibilities — like helping with chores, supporting one another, and contributing to decisions — that keep the family functioning well.

lessons.title: Crab Walk Relay and Agawang Sulok
lessons.sub: Iring-iring or Laglag Panyo, Siksik Bulak
learn: Crab Walk Relay is a game where players move like a crab — hands and feet on the ground, belly facing up — racing to complete a relay.
Agawang Sulok ("stealing the corner") is a game where players try to grab an open corner spot while one player without a corner tries to take theirs.
"Iring-iring" or "Laglag Panyo" (Drop the Handkerchief) is a game where a player secretly drops a handkerchief behind someone in a circle, who must then chase them.
"Siksik Bulak" is a traditional game that involves quick movement and teamwork, often played in groups.
These games help develop coordination, speed, and teamwork while keeping physical activity fun.

lessons.title: Essential Nutrients and a Balanced Meal
lessons.sub: Concept and Importance of Safe and Healthy Eating
learn: Safe and healthy eating means choosing foods that are clean, properly prepared, and provide the nutrients your body needs.
Essential nutrients include carbohydrates (energy), protein (growth and repair), fats (energy storage), vitamins, and minerals (body functions).
A balanced meal includes a mix of these nutrients, along with enough water, to keep the body functioning well.
A balanced diet over time — not just one meal — is what truly supports good health and steady growth.

lessons.title: Non-Locomotor and Locomotor Movements
lessons.sub: Fundamental Dance Movements, Fitness Concepts, Tiklos
learn: Locomotor movements move the body from one place to another, like walking, running, jumping, and skipping.
Non-locomotor movements happen in place without traveling, like bending, twisting, stretching, and swaying.
Fundamental dance movements combine locomotor and non-locomotor movements with rhythm to create dance steps.
"Tiklos" refers to a traditional Filipino practice of community members working or moving together, often incorporated into folk dance and cooperative activities.
Understanding movement and fitness concepts, like flexibility and endurance, helps people stay active and healthy.

lessons.title: Child Basic Health Rights
lessons.sub: Filipino Consumer Rights and Responsibilities, Consumer Skills
learn: Every child has basic health rights, including the right to nutritious food, clean water, medical care, and a safe environment.
As consumers, Filipinos have rights such as the right to safety, the right to be informed, and the right to choose products wisely.
Along with these rights come responsibilities — like reading labels carefully, using products safely, and reporting unsafe products.
Good consumer skills include comparing prices, checking expiration dates, and being cautious of misleading advertisements.

lessons.title: Health and Fitness Facts and Fads
learn: A health fact is information about health that is supported by science and evidence, like "regular exercise strengthens the heart."
A health fad is a popular trend that claims quick results but often lacks strong scientific support, like extreme diets promising instant weight loss.
It's important to be able to tell facts from fads so you can make safe, informed choices about your health and fitness.
A good way to check if health information is a fact or a fad is to see if it is supported by trusted experts, like doctors or scientists.

lessons.title: Paro-Parong Bukid
learn: "Paro-Parong Bukid" is a well-known Filipino folk dance that imitates the graceful, fluttering movement of a butterfly ("paro-paro") in the field ("bukid").
The dance is often performed by a female dancer wearing a traditional Filipino dress, using a fan to mimic butterfly wings.
Folk dances like Paro-Parong Bukid preserve Filipino culture and are often performed during school programs and cultural celebrations.
Performing folk dances also promotes physical fitness, coordination, and an appreciation for Filipino heritage.

chapters.title: Lesson 1: Internal Components of the Computer

lessons.title: What is a Computer?
learn: A computer is an electronic device that accepts data (input), processes it, and produces useful information (output).
Computers are used in many fields: schools (learning and research), hospitals (patient records), banks (transactions), and homes (entertainment and communication).

The main internal components include the CPU (Central Processing Unit, the 'brain' of the computer), motherboard (connects all parts), RAM (temporary memory for running programs), and storage drive (HDD/SSD, for saving files permanently).
The power supply unit (PSU) converts electricity into a form the computer's parts can use, while cooling fans keep the components from overheating.

lessons.title: Bits, Bytes, and Binary
lessons.sub: Data Types and Common File Size
learn: Computers store and process information using binary code — a system with only two digits, 0 and 1, called bits.
A bit is the smallest unit of data; 8 bits make up 1 byte, which is enough to represent one character, like a letter or number.
Larger amounts of data are measured in kilobytes (KB), megabytes (MB), gigabytes (GB), and terabytes (TB) — each one about 1,000 times bigger than the one before it.
Common data types include text, numbers, images, audio, and video files, each stored and displayed differently by the computer.

lessons.title: Organizing and Protecting Data
learn: Data management is the process of organizing, storing, and maintaining data so it can be easily found, used, and protected.
Good data management keeps files organized, prevents data loss, and makes it easier to find important information quickly.

Computer memory is divided into two types: primary memory (like RAM), which is temporary and fast, used while the computer is running; and secondary memory (like a hard drive or USB), which is permanent storage that keeps data even after the computer is turned off.
Backing up files regularly — saving copies in another location — is an important part of good data management.

lessons.title: Types and Characteristics of Software
learn: Software is a set of instructions or programs that tell a computer's hardware what to do.
There are two main types of software: system software (like the operating system, which manages the computer itself) and application software (like Word or games, which help users do specific tasks).
Good software should be reliable, easy to use, and able to work well with the computer's hardware.
Common software challenges include bugs (errors in the program), the need for updates, and compatibility issues (when software does not work well with certain hardware or other programs).

chapters.title: Lesson 5: Advanced Text Formatting in Microsoft Word

lessons.title: Fonts, Paragraphs, and Views
learn: Microsoft Word is a productivity tool used for creating, editing, and formatting text documents.
Font formatting includes changing the font style, size, color, and effects like bold, italic, and underline to make text look clear and appealing.
Editing paragraphs involves adjusting alignment (left, center, right, justify), line spacing, and indentation to organize text neatly.
Document views — such as Print Layout, Web Layout, and Read Mode — let users see and work on a document in different ways depending on their needs.

chapters.title: Lesson 6: Using the Insert Tab in Microsoft Word

lessons.title: Inserting Images and Tables
learn: The Insert tab in Microsoft Word allows users to add extra elements to a document, such as images, tables, shapes, and page numbers.
Inserting an image helps illustrate ideas — users can resize, move, and wrap text around pictures to fit the layout.
Inserting a table organizes information into rows and columns, which is useful for lists, schedules, or comparisons.
After inserting an image or table, formatting tools appear that let users adjust size, style, and position.

chapters.title: Lesson 7: Creating Slideshows with MS PowerPoint

lessons.title: PowerPoint Essential Tools
learn: Microsoft PowerPoint is a productivity tool used to create slideshows for presentations.
Essential PowerPoint tools include the slide layout (arranging text and images), themes (ready-made designs), and the slide sorter (for organizing slide order).
Text boxes, images, and shapes can all be added to slides to make presentations clear and engaging.
A good slideshow uses simple, readable slides with a consistent design from start to finish.

chapters.title: Lesson 8: Introduction to Data Visualization and Animation

lessons.title: Charts, Transitions, and Animations
learn: Data visualization means presenting information using charts, graphs, or diagrams instead of plain text, making it easier to understand.
PowerPoint allows users to insert charts (like bar or pie charts) to visually represent numbers and comparisons.
Transitions are effects that happen when moving from one slide to the next, while animations are effects applied to text or objects within a single slide.
Using transitions and animations sparingly makes a presentation more engaging without distracting the audience.

chapters.title: Lesson 9: Microsoft Excel Navigation and Cell Formatting

lessons.title: Navigating Excel and Formatting Cells
learn: Microsoft Excel is a productivity tool used to organize data, perform calculations, and create spreadsheets made of rows, columns, and cells.
Navigating Excel involves moving between cells using the mouse or arrow keys, and using the Name Box to jump directly to a specific cell.
Keyboard shortcuts, like Ctrl+C (copy), Ctrl+V (paste), and Ctrl+S (save), help users work faster in Excel.
The Fonts section in the Home tab lets users format cell text with different font styles, sizes, colors, and borders.

chapters.title: Lesson 10: Principles of Collaboration and Workflow

lessons.title: Working Together Effectively
learn: Collaboration means working together with others toward a common goal, sharing ideas and responsibilities.
Important aspects of collaboration include clear communication, respecting others' ideas, and dividing tasks fairly among group members.
Digital collaboration tools, such as Google Docs, Google Sheets, and shared drives, allow multiple people to work on the same file at the same time, even from different locations.
A good workflow organizes tasks in a clear order so that collaborative projects are completed efficiently.

chapters.title: Lesson 11: Google Drive User Interface and Functions

lessons.title: Navigating Google Drive
lessons.sub: Navigation Bar, Center Panel, and Main Features
learn: Google Drive is an online storage service that lets users save, organize, and share files over the internet.
The navigation bar on the left side of Google Drive provides quick access to My Drive, Shared with me, Recent files, and Trash.
The center panel displays the files and folders in the currently selected location, where users can open, rename, or organize items.
Main features of Google Drive include uploading files, creating folders, sharing files with others, and accessing files from any device with internet access.

lessons.title: Writing Emails Politely and Professionally
learn: Email etiquette refers to the polite and professional way of writing and sending emails.
A good email should have a clear subject line, a polite greeting, a short and organized message, and a proper closing.
Important email practices include checking spelling and grammar before sending, using a respectful tone, and avoiding writing in all capital letters (which can seem like shouting).
Replying to emails promptly and only including necessary recipients are also important parts of good email etiquette.

chapters.title: Lesson 13: Video Conferencing with Google Meet

lessons.title: Accessing and Using Google Meet
learn: Video conferencing is a way of communicating with others through live video and audio over the internet, even from different locations.
Google Meet can be accessed through a web browser, the Google Meet app, or through a Google Calendar event link.
Features of Google Meet include screen sharing, chat messaging, virtual backgrounds, and muting or turning off your camera during a call.
Video conferencing is useful for online classes, meetings, and staying connected with family and friends far away.

chapters.title: Lesson 14: Learning About the Basics of Coding

lessons.title: What is Coding?
lessons.sub: Common Coding Methods and Importance of Coding
learn: Coding is the process of writing instructions, called code, that tell a computer what to do step by step.

Common coding methods for beginners include block-based coding (like Scratch, where instructions are dragged and connected like puzzle pieces) and text-based coding (typing lines of code in a programming language).
Coding is important because it helps build problem-solving skills, creativity, and an understanding of how apps, games, and websites are made.
Learning to code also helps students think logically and break big problems into smaller, manageable steps.

lessons.title: Understanding Events and Sequencing
learn: In coding, an event is something that triggers a program to start doing an action, like clicking a button or pressing a key.
A sequence is the order in which instructions are carried out, one after another, from beginning to end.
Sequencing events correctly is important because a program with the wrong order of steps may not work as intended.
Real-life activities, like following a recipe step by step, are also examples of sequencing — doing things in the correct order to get the right result.

lessons.title: Navigating Scratch and Its Blocks
learn: Scratch is a free, beginner-friendly, block-based coding platform where users create programs, games, and animations by snapping blocks together.
The Scratch interface includes the stage (where the program runs), the sprite list (characters/objects in the project), and the blocks palette (where coding blocks are found).
Scratch blocks are grouped into categories such as Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, and Control, each serving a different purpose in a program.
Users build programs in Scratch by dragging blocks from the palette and snapping them together in the correct sequence.

lessons.title: Tiyak at Relatibong Lokasyon
learn: Ang heograpiya ay ang pag-aaral tungkol sa mga lugar, tao, at kapaligiran sa daigdig.
Ang mapa ay patag na larawan ng Daigdig o bahagi nito, samantalang ang globo ay tatlong-dimensyong modelo ng Daigdig.
Ang tiyak (absolute) na lokasyon ay tumutukoy sa eksaktong posisyon ng isang lugar gamit ang latitude at longitude.
Ang relatibong lokasyon naman ay ang posisyon ng isang lugar batay sa kaugnayan nito sa ibang lugar, tulad ng 'sa hilaga ng Maynila'.

lessons.title: Saligan ng Teritoryo ng Pilipinas
learn: Ang teritoryo ng Pilipinas ay binubuo ng lupa, tubig, at himpapawid na sakop ng bansa.
Ayon sa kasaysayan, sakop ng teritoryo ng Pilipinas ang mga lupaing ipinagkaloob sa ilalim ng Kasunduan sa Paris noong 1898.
Ayon sa Saligang Batas, tinutukoy ng 1987 Konstitusyon ang mga lupain, karagatan, at himpapawid na bahagi ng Pilipinas.
Ang Doktrinang Pangkapuluan (Archipelagic Doctrine) sa ilalim ng UNCLOS ay nagsasaad na ang mga katubigang nasa gitna ng mga isla ng Pilipinas ay itinuturing na panloob na katubigan ng bansa.

lessons.title: Heograpiyang Pisikal at Pantao
learn: Ang heograpiyang pisikal ay tumutukoy sa likas na katangian ng isang lugar tulad ng klima, panahon, anyong lupa, at anyong tubig.
May dalawang uri ng panahon sa Pilipinas: tag-init at tag-ulan, dulot ng monsoon at bagyo.
Kabilang sa mga anyong lupa ang bundok, kapatagan, at burol, samantalang ang anyong tubig ay may dagat, ilog, at lawa.
Ang heograpiyang pantao naman ay tumutukoy sa populasyon at mga katutubong pangkat etniko (Indigenous Peoples) na naninirahan sa isang lugar.

lessons.title: Kahalagahan sa Pag-unlad ng Bansa
learn: Ang katangiang heograpikal ng isang bansa ay may malaking epekto sa uri ng hanapbuhay, kultura, at pamumuhay ng mga mamamayan nito.
Ang mayamang likas na yaman, tulad ng masaganang lupa at karagatan, ay nagbibigay-daan sa pagsasaka, pangingisda, at turismo.
Ang lokasyon ng Pilipinas sa Pacific Ring of Fire ay nagdudulot ng mga panganib gaya ng lindol at bulkan, kaya mahalaga ang kahandaan sa sakuna.
Ang pag-unawa sa katangiang heograpikal ay tumutulong sa pamahalaan at mamamayan na magplano nang mabuti para sa kaunlaran at kaligtasan.

lessons.title: Likas na Yaman at Gawaing Pangkabuhayan
learn: Ang likas na yaman ng Pilipinas ay binubuo ng lupa, tubig, gubat, enerhiya, at mineral — samantalang ang yamang-tao ay tumutukoy sa mga mamamayang nag-aambag ng lakas-paggawa.
Kabilang sa mga gawaing pangkabuhayan ang pagsasaka, pangingisda, pagmimina, pagtotroso, at pagmamanupaktura, na nagbibigay ng kabuhayan sa maraming Pilipino.
Ang bansa ay humaharap sa mga hamon tulad ng labis na pagsasamantala sa likas na yaman at polusyon, kaya kinakailangan ang mga tugon tulad ng pagpapatupad ng batas pangkapaligiran.
Ang pangangalaga sa likas na yaman ay mahalaga upang matiyak na sapat pa rin ito para sa susunod na henerasyon.

chapters.title: B. Mga Hamon sa Pagkamit ng Likas-kayang Pag-unlad

lessons.title: Likas-kayang Pag-unlad
learn: Ang likas-kayang pag-unlad ay ang uri ng pag-unlad na sumasagot sa pangangailangan ng kasalukuyang henerasyon nang hindi isinasakripisyo ang kakayahan ng susunod na henerasyon na sagutin ang kanilang sariling pangangailangan.
Kabilang sa mga hamon sa likas-kayang pag-unlad ang polusyon, deforestation, at labis na paggamit ng likas na yaman.
Ang pagbabago ng klima (climate change) ay isa ring malaking hamon na nakaaapekto sa agrikultura at kabuhayan ng mga Pilipino.
Ang mga solusyon ay kinabibilangan ng responsableng paggamit ng yaman, pagtatanim muli ng puno, at pagpapatupad ng mahigpit na batas pangkapaligiran.

lessons.title: Apat na Elemento ng Pagkabansa
learn: Ang isang bansa ay binubuo ng apat na elemento: tao (mamamayan), teritoryo (lupain), pamahalaan, at soberanya (kapangyarihang mamuno nang independiyente).
Ang tao o mamamayan ay ang mga taong naninirahan sa bansa at bumubuo sa lipunan nito.
Ang teritoryo ay ang lupain, tubig, at himpapawid na sakop ng bansa.
Ang soberanya ay ang kapangyarihan ng isang bansa na mamahala sa sarili nitong mga usapin nang malaya sa ibang bansa.

lessons.title: Unitary Presidential System at Separation of Powers
learn: Ang Pilipinas ay may unitary presidential system ng pamahalaan, kung saan nagtataglay ang Pangulo ng malaking kapangyarihan bilang pinuno ng estado at pamahalaan.
Sa unitary system, ang kapangyarihan ay nasa sentral na pamahalaan, bagamat may mga tungkuling ipinagkakaloob sa mga lokal na yunit ng pamahalaan.
Ang separation of powers ay ang paghahati ng kapangyarihan ng pamahalaan sa tatlong sangay: Ehekutibo, Lehislatibo, at Hudisyal.
Layunin ng separation of powers na maiwasan ang labis na kapangyarihan sa isang sangay lamang, upang magkaroon ng tsek at balanse (checks and balances).

lessons.title: Serbisyong Panlipunan, Pang-ekonomiya, at Pangkalahatan
lessons.sub: Batay sa Pambansang Badyet ng Pilipinas
learn: Ang serbisyong panlipunan ng pamahalaan ay sumasaklaw sa edukasyon, kalusugan, at panlipunang kaligtasan, kagalingan, at empleyo ng mga mamamayan.
Ang serbisyong pang-ekonomiya naman ay kinabibilangan ng komunikasyon, mga kalsada at transportasyon, agrikultura, at pagpapaunlad ng yamang tubig.
Ang pangkalahatang serbisyong publiko ay tumutugon sa kaayusang publiko, kaligtasan, at pangkalahatang administrasyon ng bansa.
Ang mga serbisyong ito ay ibinabatay sa Pambansang Badyet ng Pilipinas, na nagtatakda kung magkano ang ilalaan sa bawat sektor.

chapters.title: A. Mga Sagisag ng Pagkakakilanlang Pilipino

lessons.title: Mga Pambansang Sagisag
learn: Ang mga sagisag ng pagkakakilanlang Pilipino ay kumakatawan sa kultura, kasaysayan, at pagkakaisa ng bansa.
Kabilang sa mga pambansang sagisag ang watawat ng Pilipinas, pambansang awit (Lupang Hinirang), at pambansang bulaklak (sampaguita).
Ang mga sagisag na ito ay dapat igalang, dahil sumisimbolo sila sa kalayaan at pagkakakilanlan ng bansa.
Ang pagpapahalaga sa mga pambansang sagisag ay isang paraan ng pagpapakita ng pagmamahal sa bayan.

lessons.title: Ano ang Pagkamamamayan?
learn: Ang pagkamamamayan ay ang legal na katayuan ng isang tao bilang kinikilalang miyembro ng isang bansa, kalakip ang mga karapatan at tungkulin.
Ang isang tao ay maaaring maging mamamayang Pilipino sa pamamagitan ng kapanganakan (natural-born) o sa pamamagitan ng naturalisasyon.
Bilang mamamayan, may tinatamasang karapatan ang isang tao, ngunit mayroon ding tungkuling dapat tuparin para sa ikabubuti ng bansa.
Ang pagiging responsableng mamamayan ay nangangahulugan ng pagsunod sa batas at pakikilahok sa ikauunlad ng komunidad.

chapters.title: C. Karapatan at Tungkulin ng Mamamayang Pilipino

lessons.title: Uri ng Karapatan at Kaakibat na Tungkulin
learn: Ang karapatan ay ang mga bagay na dapat tamasahin ng bawat mamamayan, na protektado ng batas at Saligang Batas.

May tatlong uri ng karapatan: karapatang sibil (tulad ng kalayaan sa pananalita), karapatang politikal (tulad ng karapatang bumoto), at karapatang panlipunan at pangkabuhayan (tulad ng karapatan sa edukasyon at trabaho).
Bawat karapatan ay may kaakibat na tungkulin — halimbawa, ang karapatang bumoto ay may kaakibat na tungkuling bumoto nang matalino at responsable.
Ang pagkilala at pagtupad sa parehong karapatan at tungkulin ay mahalaga upang mapanatili ang kaayusan at kaunlaran ng lipunan.

lessons.title: Place Value and Value
lessons.sub: Reading and Writing Numbers up to 1,000,000
learn: Place value tells us WHERE a digit sits in a number (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, millions); value tells us WHAT that digit is actually worth there.
In the number 763,245: 7 is in the hundred thousands place (value 700,000), 6 is in the ten thousands place (value 60,000), and 5 is in the ones place (value 5).

To read a large number, split it into periods of three digits using commas, then read each group followed by its period name — for example 452,678 is read 'four hundred fifty-two thousand, six hundred seventy-eight.'
When writing numbers in words, spell out each period completely and only say 'and' if there is a decimal point — not between whole number periods.

lessons.title: Comparing, Ordering, and Rounding
lessons.sub: Rounding to the Nearest Hundred Thousand
learn: To compare two whole numbers, first compare the number of digits — more digits usually means a bigger number — then compare digits from the leftmost place value.
The symbols > (greater than), < (less than), and = (equal to) are used to compare numbers, such as 542,300 > 524,300.
To order numbers, arrange them from least to greatest (ascending) or greatest to least (descending) by comparing their place values step by step.
To round a number to the nearest hundred thousand, look at the ten thousands digit: if it's 5 or more, round up; if it's less than 5, round down and replace the remaining digits with zeros.

chapters.title: B. Operations of Whole Numbers with Problem Solving

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction of Whole Numbers
learn: Addition combines two or more numbers into a total called the sum; regrouping (carrying) happens when a column's total is 10 or more, so we carry the extra ten to the next column.
Subtraction finds the difference between numbers; regrouping (borrowing) happens when a digit on top is smaller than the digit below it, so we borrow 1 from the next place value.
Always line up numbers by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens) before adding or subtracting to avoid mistakes.
You can check subtraction by adding the difference and the number subtracted — the result should equal the original number.

lessons.title: Multiplication of Whole Numbers
learn: Multiplication is repeated addition — 4 × 3 means adding 4 three times (4 + 4 + 4 = 12).

When multiplying multi-digit numbers, multiply by each place value separately (ones, then tens, then hundreds), shifting each partial product one place to the left, then add the partial products together.
Any number multiplied by 0 equals 0, and any number multiplied by 1 stays the same — these are called the zero property and identity property of multiplication.
Estimating a product first (by rounding factors) helps check whether your final answer is reasonable.

lessons.title: Division of Whole Numbers
learn: Division splits a number (the dividend) into equal groups based on the divisor, giving a quotient — and sometimes a remainder if it doesn't divide evenly.
Long division follows the steps: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down — repeated for each digit of the dividend.
You can check a division answer by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding any remainder; the result should equal the dividend.
A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor — if it isn't, the division wasn't finished correctly.

chapters.title: C. Order of Operations and Estimation

lessons.title: Order of Operations (MDAS)
learn: MDAS stands for Multiplication, Division, Addition, Subtraction — the order we follow when a problem has more than one operation.
Multiplication and division are performed first, working from left to right; then addition and subtraction are performed, also from left to right.
Operations inside grouping symbols like parentheses ( ) should be solved first, before applying MDAS to the rest of the expression.
Following the correct order matters — solving operations in the wrong order can give a completely different (and wrong) answer.

lessons.title: Estimation of Whole Numbers
lessons.sub: Estimating Sums, Differences, Products, and Quotients
learn: Estimation means finding an answer that is close to the exact one, often by rounding numbers first to make calculations quicker and easier.
To estimate a sum or difference, round each number to the same place value (like the nearest thousand), then add or subtract the rounded numbers.
To estimate a product, round the factors to their greatest place value before multiplying — this gives a quick, reasonable answer.
Estimation is useful for checking if an exact answer is reasonable, and for quick mental math when an exact answer isn't needed.

lessons.title: Factors and Multiples
learn: A factor is a number that divides another number exactly, with no remainder — for example, 3 is a factor of 12 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4 exactly.
A multiple is the result of multiplying a number by a whole number — the multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and so on.
Every number is both a factor and a multiple of itself, and 1 is a factor of every whole number.
To find all factors of a number, test which whole numbers divide into it evenly, usually checking up to its square root.

lessons.title: GCF and LCM
lessons.sub: Greatest Common Factor and Least Common Denominator
learn: The Greatest Common Factor (GCF) is the largest number that divides evenly into two or more numbers — for 12 and 18, the GCF is 6.
The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers — for 4 and 6, the LCM is 12.
To find the GCF, list the factors of each number and pick the greatest one they share; to find the LCM, list multiples of each number and pick the smallest one they share.
The Least Common Denominator (LCD) used when adding or subtracting fractions is simply the LCM of the denominators.

lessons.title: Types of Fractions
learn: A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator (like 3/4), meaning it represents less than one whole.
An improper fraction has a numerator equal to or greater than its denominator (like 7/4), meaning it represents one whole or more.
A mixed number combines a whole number and a proper fraction (like 1¾), which is another way to write an improper fraction.
To change an improper fraction to a mixed number, divide the numerator by the denominator — the quotient is the whole number and the remainder becomes the new numerator.

lessons.title: Fractions on a Number Line and Equivalent Fractions
learn: Fractions can be plotted on a number line by dividing the space between whole numbers into equal parts based on the denominator.
Equivalent fractions represent the same value even though they look different, like 1/2 and 2/4 — they land on the same point on a number line.
To find an equivalent fraction, multiply (or divide) both the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.
Reducing a fraction to simplest form means dividing the numerator and denominator by their GCF until no common factor remains.

lessons.title: Comparing and Ordering Dissimilar Fractions
learn: Dissimilar fractions have different denominators, like 1/3 and 1/4, which makes them harder to compare directly.
To compare dissimilar fractions, first find a common denominator (often the LCD), rewrite each fraction, then compare their numerators.
Once fractions share the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is the greater fraction.
Ordering dissimilar fractions from least to greatest follows the same process: convert to a common denominator first, then arrange by numerator.

chapters.title: C. Operations of Fractions with Problem-Solving

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction of Similar Fractions
learn: Similar fractions share the same denominator, so adding or subtracting them just means adding or subtracting the numerators and keeping the denominator the same.
For mixed numbers with similar fractions, add or subtract the whole numbers and the fractional parts separately, then combine the results.
If subtracting mixed numbers and the fraction on top is smaller than the one being subtracted, borrow 1 whole from the whole number and convert it into a fraction.
Always simplify the final answer to its lowest terms, and convert an improper fraction result into a mixed number if needed.

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction of Dissimilar Fractions
learn: Dissimilar fractions have different denominators, so before adding or subtracting them you must first rewrite them with a common denominator (usually the LCD).
Once the fractions share a common denominator, add or subtract the numerators as usual and keep the denominator the same.
Multi-step word problems involving fractions may require more than one operation — read carefully to determine whether to add, subtract, or both.
Always double-check your final fraction answer is in simplest form, and convert improper fractions to mixed numbers when appropriate.

chapters.title: A. Decimal Numbers up to Hundredths

lessons.title: Concept of Decimals
lessons.sub: Converting Decimals to Fractions and Vice Versa
learn: A decimal is another way to show a part of a whole, using a decimal point — the first place after the point is tenths, and the second is hundredths.
To convert a decimal to a fraction, use the decimal digits as the numerator and a power of 10 (10 for tenths, 100 for hundredths) as the denominator, then simplify.
To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator, or rewrite the fraction with a denominator of 10 or 100.
On a number line, decimals are placed the same way as fractions — 0.5 sits exactly halfway between 0 and 1.

lessons.title: Reading, Writing, Comparing, Ordering, and Rounding Decimals
learn: Decimals are read using the place value of the last digit — 0.45 is read 'forty-five hundredths,' since the 5 is in the hundredths place.
To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare digit by digit starting from the leftmost place value, treating missing digits as zero.
To order decimals, compare them the same way as whole numbers once the decimal points are aligned.
To round a decimal to the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: if it's 5 or more, round the tenths digit up; if less than 5, keep the tenths digit the same.

lessons.title: Simple Patterns and Number Sentences
learn: A number pattern is a sequence of numbers that follows a specific rule, such as adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing by the same amount each time.
To find the rule of a pattern, look at how each number changes to become the next one in the sequence.
A number sentence is a mathematical statement using numbers and symbols (like +, −, ×, ÷, =) to show a relationship, such as 8 + ☐ = 15.
Solving a number sentence with a missing number means figuring out what value makes the equation true, often by using the inverse (opposite) operation.

lessons.title: Types of Angles
learn: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common point called the vertex, and its size is measured in degrees.
An acute angle measures less than 90°, a right angle measures exactly 90°, and an obtuse angle measures more than 90° but less than 180°.
A straight angle measures exactly 180°, forming a straight line, while a reflex angle measures more than 180° but less than 360°.
You can often identify the general type of angle just by looking at how 'open' or 'closed' it appears compared to a right angle (a perfect corner).

lessons.title: Measuring and Constructing Angles
learn: A protractor is a tool used to measure and draw angles, marked with two rows of numbers from 0° to 180°.
To measure an angle, place the protractor's center point exactly on the vertex, and line up the base line with one ray of the angle at 0°.
Read the degree where the second ray crosses the protractor's scale, making sure to use the correct row of numbers (inner or outer) depending on which side you started from.
To construct an angle of a given measure, draw a ray, place the protractor's center on the ray's endpoint, mark the correct degree, then draw a second ray connecting that point to the vertex.

lessons.title: Symmetric Figures and Reflection
learn: A figure has symmetry if it can be folded along a line so both halves match exactly — that fold line is called the line of symmetry.
Some figures have more than one line of symmetry, like a square (4 lines) or a circle (infinite lines), while others have none at all.
Reflection is a transformation that flips a figure over a line, creating a mirror image that is the same size and shape but faces the opposite direction.
In a reflection, every point on the original figure has a matching point on the mirror image that is the same distance from the line of reflection.

lessons.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals
learn: A triangle is a polygon with 3 sides and 3 angles, and the sum of its interior angles always equals 180°.
A quadrilateral is a polygon with 4 sides and 4 angles, and the sum of its interior angles always equals 360°.
Properties like side length, angle measure, and parallel sides help distinguish one type of triangle or quadrilateral from another.
Polygons are named based on their number of sides, and both triangles and quadrilaterals are classified further by their specific properties.

lessons.title: Classification According to Sides and Angles
learn: Triangles can be classified by sides: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (two sides equal), and scalene (no sides equal).
Triangles can also be classified by angles: acute triangle (all angles less than 90°), right triangle (one 90° angle), and obtuse triangle (one angle more than 90°).

Quadrilaterals can be classified by their properties: a square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles; a rectangle has 4 right angles with opposite sides equal; a parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal.
Other quadrilaterals include the rhombus (4 equal sides, opposite angles equal), the trapezoid (only one pair of parallel sides), and the kite (two pairs of adjacent equal sides).

lessons.title: Perimeter of Quadrilaterals and Composite Figures
learn: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape, found by adding the lengths of all its sides.
For a rectangle, perimeter = 2 × (length + width); for a square, perimeter = 4 × side length, since all sides are equal.

A composite figure is made up of two or more basic shapes combined together; to find its perimeter, add the lengths of all outer sides, being careful not to include any inner lines that aren't part of the outside boundary.
Always make sure all side measurements are in the same unit before adding them together to find the perimeter.

lessons.title: Conversion and Measurement of Units
learn: Length is commonly measured in millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers; common conversions include 1 meter = 100 centimeters and 1 kilometer = 1,000 meters.
Mass is commonly measured in grams and kilograms, where 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams.
Capacity (the amount of liquid a container can hold) is commonly measured in milliliters and liters, where 1 liter = 1,000 milliliters.
Time is measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, and years — common conversions include 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, and 24 hours = 1 day.

lessons.title: Tabular Form and Single Line Graph
learn: Data collection means gathering information, often through surveys, observations, or measurements, to answer a specific question.
A table organizes collected data into rows and columns, making it easy to compare values and spot patterns at a glance.
A single line graph uses points connected by a line to show how data changes over time, such as temperature readings across a week.
Interpreting data means reading a table or graph carefully to answer questions, such as finding the highest value, the lowest value, or how much something increased or decreased.

gmrc.title: Forming One's Awareness Toward Good Behaviors

chapters.title: A. I Can Think and Love as a Unique Person

lessons.title: I Can Think and Love as a Unique Person
lessons.sub: Ways to Be Unique, 7 Important Social Skills
learn: Every person is unique — no one else has exactly the same combination of thoughts, feelings, talents, and personality as you.
You can grow into a more unique, well-rounded person by discovering your interests, being kind, staying curious, and being true to your own values instead of just copying others.
Important social skills for children include listening well, sharing, taking turns, showing empathy, cooperating, resolving conflicts peacefully, and respecting others' feelings.
Thinking for yourself and loving others are both signs of good character — they help you make good choices and build strong relationships.

chapters.title: B. I Value My Good Relationship with My Family

lessons.title: I Value My Good Relationship with My Family
lessons.sub: Features and Qualities of a Strong Family Relationship
learn: A strong family relationship is built on important features like trust, open communication, mutual respect, and spending quality time together.
Families with strong relationships support each other through difficulties, celebrate each other's successes, and forgive one another when mistakes happen.
Qualities like honesty, patience, love, and cooperation help strengthen the bond between family members over time.
Valuing your family relationship means actively contributing to it — through kindness, helping with chores, and showing appreciation for each family member.

chapters.title: C. I Respect the Rights of My Fellow Child

lessons.title: I Respect the Rights of My Fellow Child
lessons.sub: Ways to Show Respect for the Rights of Fellow Children
learn: Every child has rights, such as the right to be safe, to be treated fairly, to express their opinions, and to be free from bullying or harm.
Respecting the rights of fellow children means treating them kindly, listening to their opinions, and never excluding or teasing them unfairly.
Standing up for a friend who is being treated unfairly is one way to actively respect and protect the rights of other children.
Respecting others' rights also means respecting their differences — such as different abilities, backgrounds, or ways of thinking.

chapters.title: D. I Value My Faith in God

lessons.title: I Value My Faith in God
lessons.sub: What Children Should Learn About Faith, Virtues that Strengthen Faith
learn: Faith means believing in and trusting God, even when we cannot see Him, and expressing that trust through prayer and good actions.
Children can learn about faith through prayer, attending religious activities, reading about their faith, and observing the good example of family members.
Virtues like hope, trust, gratitude, and love help strengthen a person's faith in God over time.
Living out one's faith means showing kindness, honesty, and love toward others — not just believing quietly, but putting faith into action.

chapters.title: E. I Am a Good Steward of Our Environment

lessons.title: I Am a Good Steward of Our Environment
lessons.sub: Caring for Plants and Trees, Types and Importance of Being a Steward
learn: Being a good steward of the environment means taking responsibility for caring for and protecting nature, including plants, trees, and surroundings.
Ways to take care of the environment include watering plants, avoiding littering, properly disposing of waste, and planting trees.
There are different types of environmental stewards: some protect wildlife, some conserve resources like water and energy, and some educate others about caring for nature.
Being a good steward is important because it helps preserve natural resources for future generations and keeps ecosystems healthy and balanced.

chapters.title: F. I Help Preserve Our Filipino Values

lessons.title: I Help Preserve Our Filipino Values
learn: Filipino values are traditional beliefs and practices passed down through generations, such as 'paggalang' (respect), 'pakikisama' (getting along with others), and 'utang na loob' (gratitude/debt of gratitude).
Other important Filipino values include 'bayanihan' (community spirit and helping one another) and 'malasakit' (compassion and genuine concern for others).
Helping preserve Filipino values means practicing them in daily life — showing respect to elders, helping neighbors, and being grateful for kindness shown to you.
Filipino values help unite communities and strengthen family bonds, making them an important part of Filipino identity and culture.

gmrc.title: The Family as Guide in Developing Good Behaviors

chapters.title: A. I Am Confident in Exhibiting My Talents

lessons.title: I Am Confident in Exhibiting My Talents
lessons.sub: Exploring Talents, 9 Types of Multiple Intelligences
learn: Parents and teachers can help children explore their talents by exposing them to different activities, encouraging their interests, and praising their effort.

The theory of Multiple Intelligences identifies 9 types of intelligence, including linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic, and existential intelligence.
Every child is intelligent in different ways — some excel in math and logic, others in music, movement, understanding people, or connecting with nature.
Children need supportive relationships, encouragement, and opportunities for practice to fully develop their talents and abilities.

chapters.title: B. I Accomplish My Tasks Well

lessons.title: I Accomplish My Tasks Well
learn: Children can accomplish age-appropriate household tasks such as making their bed, arranging their things, helping set the table, and doing simple cleaning.
Doing household tasks well teaches children responsibility, discipline, and the value of contributing to the family.
Completing tasks well means doing them carefully, on time, and without needing to be reminded repeatedly.
Children who accomplish their tasks well build good habits that help them succeed in school and in life as they grow older.

chapters.title: C. I Communicate Well with Others

lessons.title: I Communicate Well with Others
lessons.sub: Kinds of Communication, Ways to Communicate with Others
learn: Communication can be verbal (spoken or written words) or non-verbal (facial expressions, gestures, tone of voice, and body language).
Good communication involves not just speaking clearly, but also listening carefully and paying attention to what others are saying.
Ways to communicate well with others include being polite, making eye contact, using kind words, and waiting for your turn to speak.
Good communication helps prevent misunderstandings and builds stronger, more trusting relationships with family, friends, and others.

chapters.title: D. I Practice Faith within My Family

lessons.title: I Practice Faith within My Family
lessons.sub: Things the Family Should Do Regularly, Ways to Invite God, Enemies of Faith
learn: Families can practice faith together by praying regularly, attending religious services together, and reading about their faith as a family.
Inviting God into the home can be done through daily prayer, giving thanks before meals, and keeping kind and honest conversations at home.
Enemies of faith include things that weaken a person's trust in God, such as doubt, pride, greed, and constantly making bad choices without seeking forgiveness.
A family that practices faith together tends to build stronger bonds, greater peace, and better guidance for making good decisions.

chapters.title: E. I Help My Family Conserve Water

lessons.title: I Help My Family Conserve Water
lessons.sub: Ways to Conserve Clean Water for Future Generations
learn: Water conservation means using water wisely and avoiding waste so that clean water remains available for people and the environment in the future.
Simple ways to conserve water at home include turning off the faucet while brushing teeth, fixing leaks promptly, and taking shorter showers.
Reusing water when possible, such as using leftover water for plants, is another way families can help conserve this important resource.
Children play an important role in water conservation by practicing good habits and reminding family members to avoid wasting water.

chapters.title: F. I Strengthen My Nationalism with My Family

lessons.title: I Strengthen My Nationalism with My Family
lessons.sub: Filipino Family Customs, Improving Negative Customs, Promoting Good Customs
learn: Filipino families have many customs, such as 'mano po' (a gesture of respect to elders), family gatherings during holidays, and close family ties across generations.
Some Filipino customs, like excessive 'utang na loob' pressure or 'crab mentality,' can be negative and may need to be improved for healthier relationships.
Families can strengthen and promote good Filipino customs by practicing them consistently, teaching them to younger generations, and celebrating Filipino traditions together.
Strengthening nationalism within the family means taking pride in Filipino culture, language, and traditions while working to improve customs that may cause harm.

gmrc.title: Nurturing Good Behaviors for and with Our Neighbors

lessons.title: I Am Thrifty
lessons.sub: Defining Thriftiness, How Thriftiness Benefits Others
learn: Thriftiness means using money, time, and resources wisely, avoiding waste, and saving for future needs instead of spending carelessly.
Being thrifty involves practices like saving allowance money, reusing items when possible, and thinking carefully before making a purchase.
Thriftiness benefits others because resources saved can be shared with those in need, and wise use of shared resources leaves more for the whole community.
A thrifty person plans ahead and distinguishes between wants and needs, choosing to prioritize what is truly necessary.

chapters.title: B. I Will Fulfill My Family's Responsibility to Help Others

lessons.title: I Will Fulfill My Family's Responsibility to Help Others
lessons.sub: Examples and Importance of Fulfilling Family Responsibilities
learn: Families have a responsibility to help others, such as assisting neighbors in need, donating to charity, or volunteering for community projects.
Examples of fulfilling this responsibility include sharing food with less fortunate neighbors, helping during emergencies, and supporting community clean-up drives.
Fulfilling family responsibilities to help others strengthens community bonds and teaches children the value of compassion and generosity.
When families model helpfulness, children learn to carry these values forward into their own future relationships and communities.

chapters.title: C. I Value Equal Rights among People

lessons.title: I Value Equal Rights among People
lessons.sub: Promoting Equal Rights, Importance of Respecting the Rights of Others
